  age: 35

  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
Niran was thirty-two when his breathing simply stopped making sense. One afternoon in his Santa Monica apartment, a sudden tightness seized his chest, followed by a wave of dizziness that left him collapsed on the kitchen floor. The first responders arrived with blue lights cutting through his blinds, and within an hour he was strapped to a gurney, watching the hospital ceiling tiles blur as a breathing tube was guided down his throat. For twelve days, he drifted in and out of sedation, anchored to monitors that beeped without rhythm, learning that his own body could turn against him without warning. When he was finally discharged, the cardiologists called it a near-miss, a rare arrhythmic event that had stopped his heart long enough to scar him. He went home, but the quiet of his married life with his wife, Lan, felt suddenly thin, like paper stretched over a draft. Over the next several months, Niran’s nervous system never settled. His shoulders stayed hunched beneath his collar, his jaw clenched tight until his temples throbbed, and he lay awake most nights waiting for another collapse, certain his body was just a coiled spring. When he waited for anything—a software update, a reply to an email, the kettle to boil—he would immediately picture the worst outcome unfolding. If Lan told him he was fine, that the doctors had cleared him, he would nod but feel nothing in his chest; the reassurance slid off him like water on glass. He came to believe that something was fundamentally wrong with him, that he was running on fragile wiring. The more he tried to rest, the more hollow he felt, watching Lan laugh at her phone or point out the blooming jacaranda in their yard, while his own emotions felt sealed behind thick glass. He started making choices that quietly shrunk his world. He stopped going to the gym and refused to take the stairs, avoiding any activity that raised his heart rate or made his muscles burn. When a friend mentioned a routine check-up, or when a white coat caught his peripheral vision on the street, Niran would excuse himself to another room. Thinking about the hospital stay, the beeping monitors, the tube down his throat, made his stomach turn, so he learned to change the subject whenever his health came up. At work, where he led a team of UX designers in a glass-walled studio near downtown, these habits took root in the open-plan floor. He could no longer sit through long design sprints without standing up to pace, and he stopped volunteering for usability testing sessions because the sterile air of the lab, the sight of a colleague’s clipboard, and the sharp beep of a defibrillator charger on a desk triggered a sudden spike of panic. He began leaving early to avoid traffic, assuming a late project milestone meant something terrible had gone wrong. The distance grew between him and Lan; she stopped asking him to help plan their anniversary trip, and he stopped initiating conversation, convinced he was too fragile to carry anything more. Now, at thirty-five, Niran sits in a therapist’s office because Lan gently but firmly told him he was drowning and asked him to fight for himself. He came hoping to understand why his body still feels like a borrowed armor he cannot take off, and what he is most afraid of is not the illness returning, but the quiet realization that he is permanently fractured. He does not know how to unlearn the flinch at a siren or how to let someone else’s voice convince him he is safe when his own nerves keep screaming otherwise. He only knows he wants to stop walking away from the things that used to make him feel alive.
